newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy looks for an end to revolving-door government.
newsitem.headline: Italy looks for an end to revolving-door government.

text.p: Italy moved on Wednesday to try to end its infamous system of revolving-door governments that has given the country no fewer than 55 administrations since World War Two.

Plagued by political instability ever since the post-war constitution sought to make sure no-one could ever again be as powerful as dictator Benito Mussolini, Italy's modern governments have lasted an average of just 11 months.
Proposals being considered revolve around strengthening the role of either the president or prime minister.
The head of an all-party parliamentary commission on constitutional reform, Massimo D'Alema, outlined his ideas in a detailed, two-hour speech.

D'Alema, leader of the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), summed up progress by four sub-commissions in making proposals to be voted on in coming weeks. The commission has six more weeks to complete its work.
One of the key issues in the so-called bicameral commission, set up in February, concerns how Italy's president and prime minister should be elected.
At present, presidents are elected by parliament and they in turn appoint prime ministers after consulting political parties.

D'Alema said in an address to the first full session of the commission that the idea of a prime minister chosen directly by the people as leader of a majority was more politically acceptable than a directly-elected president.
Centre-left forces, now in power, back a proposal whereby parties making up electoral coalitions would identify their candidate for prime minister before elections.
Thus, Italians voting for parliamentarians in electoral coalitions would indirectly choose the prime minister.
Centre-left parties also want to empower the prime minister to dissolve parliament in case of a vote of no-confidence against him or her. D'Alema backed this.
Under the current constitution, parliaments are dissolved by the president, who then calls early elections.
The opposition centre-right wants Italy's president to be elected directly by the people instead of by parliament and to have a more direct role in government decisions.

"I believe there is today a greater consensus around... 'prime ministerial government,'" D'Alema said, adding that the election of the president should however be broadened to a parliamentary assembly including regional representatives.
Reform of Italy's 1948 constitution is one of the toughest political challenges facing the country.
There have been three general elections since 1992 in the upheavals that followed the exposure of entrenched political corruption and the collapse of the old governing class.
Two previous attempts to change the way Italy works have failed in the past 15 years and deep differences divide the opposing blocs on the best blueprint for reform.
The separatist Northern League, which withdrew its six members from the commission in February to press demands for federalist reform, declined to re-join for the final phase.
D'Alema said after a meeting with leader Umberto Bossi that the party had not changed its position.
The League, which has declared a symbolic independent northern "republic", wants a referendum on secession.

Federalist reform and tax decentralisation have been the subject of one of the sub-commissions and D'Alema said regions should have a form of fiscal autonomy with each region choosing its own form of local government and electoral system.
D'Alema said both houses of parliament should be streamlined, with the number of members scaled back.
The commission must report to parliament by the end of June. Both houses are then expected to spend a year studying proposals and drawing up a package of changes to put to a referendum.
